result: After 7 days of cohabitation, male mandarin voles showed significantly higher dopamine (DA) release in the NAc shell when sniffing their partner compared to sniffing a stranger, as measured by fiber photometry with dLight1.1 DA sensor (Claims C1, C54, C55).
evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about statistical analyses for photometry data. One reviewer noted 'the photometry data comparing emissions during partner vs stranger investigation over time would be best performed as a two-way ANOVA with odor type and time being separate variables' and suggested 'area-under-the-curve calculation' instead of averaging deltaF/F during 4-second windows. The editor noted 'some concerns remain about the statistical analyses,' indicating the evidence is not fully convincing as presented.

result: After 7 days of cohabitation, D2 MSNs activity in the NAc shell was significantly lower when male voles sniffed their partner compared to sniffing a stranger, as measured by fiber photometry with GCaMP6m (Claims C3, C68, C69).
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the strength of the photometry approach, they raised statistical concerns applicable to all photometry data. Additionally, one reviewer noted confusion about how 'a relative increase in excitation of D2-MSNs in the slice (Fig. 4J) is associated with an increased inhibition in vivo (Fig. 2H),' indicating the in vivo findings don't clearly align with ex vivo data and require better explanation.

result: After 7 days of cohabitation, D1 MSNs activity in the NAc shell was significantly higher when male voles sniffed their partner compared to sniffing a stranger, as measured by fiber photometry with GCaMP6m (Claims C2, C70, C71).
evaluation: Similar to DA and D2 MSN findings, reviewers raised statistical concerns about the photometry analyses. The same issues regarding appropriate statistical tests (two-way ANOVA vs. t-tests) and calculation methods (area-under-curve vs. average deltaF/F) apply to these D1 MSN activity measurements, making the evidence uncertain as currently analyzed.

result: Pair bonding induced increased excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in D2 MSNs, with higher sEPSC frequency and amplitude, higher sIPSC frequency, and an increased excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) ratio in paired males compared to naive males (Claims C72, C73, C75).
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly noted that 'the slice physiology experiments provide some interesting outcomes but it is unclear how they can be linked to the in vivo physiological outcomes and some of the outcomes don't match intuitively.' The reviewer specifically questioned why increased E/I ratio in slices (Fig. 4J) corresponds with increased inhibition in vivo (Fig. 2H), and this concern was not adequately addressed in revision.

result: Pair bonding induced decreased excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in D1 MSNs, with reduced sEPSC frequency and amplitude, and reduced sIPSC frequency (but not amplitude) in paired males compared to naive males (Claims C78, C79).
evaluation: While the slice physiology data are presented, reviewers expressed general concern that 'it is unclear how they can be linked to the in vivo physiological outcomes.' The relationship between these ex vivo synaptic changes and the in vivo D1 MSN activity increases during partner sniffing lacks clear mechanistic explanation, as noted by reviewers.

result: Chemogenetic inhibition of VP-projecting D2 MSNs in the NAc shell enhanced pair bond formation, while chemogenetic activation blocked partner preference after 7 days of cohabitation (Claims C6, C7, C88, C89).
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the strength of 'chemogenetic manipulation studies to address circuit involvement in pair bond formation' and noted 'the relationship between D2-MSN and pair bond formation is quite clear (inhibition facilitates while excitation inhibits pair bond formation).' The causal manipulation data are treated as convincing evidence for D2 MSN involvement.

result: Both chemogenetic inhibition and activation of VP-projecting D1 MSNs in the NAc shell disrupted pair bond formation, with activation showing stronger effects in blocking partner preference after 7 days of cohabitation (Claims C91, C92).
evaluation: One reviewer noted 'the role of D1-MSNs is more complicated since both excitation and inhibition disrupts pair bond formation. This is not convincingly discussed.' In revision, the reviewer reiterated: 'the response provided does not address my question. Please focus on discussing why both excitation and inhibition of D1-MSNs can disrupt pair bond formation (Figure 7).' This indicates the findings lack adequate mechanistic explanation.

result: Viral targeting using short promoters for D1 and D2 receptors showed 84-86% specificity for the intended receptor type, but also showed cross-labeling with approximately 14-20% of cells expressing the opposite receptor mRNA (Claims C64, C65, C108, C109).
evaluation: One reviewer noted 'a large set of experiments within the manuscript are dependent on using short promoters for D1 and D2 receptors in viral vectors. As the authors acknowledge this approach can lead to ectopic expression and the presented immunohistochemistry supports this notion.' The reviewer stated 'the presented quantification underestimates the degree of ectopic expression that is observed by eye,' though considered this a 'minor' concern given the distinct outcomes.

result: No significant change in intrinsic excitability of D2 MSNs was detected between naive males and paired males in current-clamp recordings (Claim C74).
evaluation: This negative finding is presented with appropriate statistical analysis and is not questioned by reviewers. It serves as a control showing that not all electrophysiological properties change with pair bonding.

result: Bath-applied dopamine (5 μM) differentially affected synaptic transmission in naive versus paired voles: DA decreased D2 sEPSC and increased D1 sEPSC in naive males, but had no significant effect in paired males (Claims C76, C77, C82, C83).
evaluation: These pharmacological experiments in slices are not specifically critiqued by reviewers and provide supporting evidence for altered DA responsiveness after pair bonding. The data complement the in vivo findings, though reviewers noted general concerns about linking slice to in vivo data.

result: After 7 days of cohabitation with females, male mandarin voles showed significant preference for their partners in a partner preference test, displaying reliable pair bonding (Claim C51).
evaluation: This behavioral validation is not questioned by reviewers and establishes the basic model. Reviewers acknowledged 'the experimental designs are strong' and the behavioral paradigm is standard for pair bonding research.

result: CNO application effectively modulated neuronal activity in DREADD-transfected neurons, with Gq-DREADD increasing action potentials and Gi-DREADD decreasing membrane potentials (Claims C85, C86).
evaluation: These validation experiments for chemogenetic tools are standard controls and are not questioned by reviewers. They demonstrate the technical efficacy of the manipulation approach.
